name: Salt River
agency: USFS Tonto National Forest / White Mountain Apache Tribe

camps.name: First Campground
camps.desc: The put-in camp, with separate public and outfitter launches. Good for the night before.

camps.name: Second Campground
camps.desc: A designated primitive tribal campground, popular with outfitters on day trips.

rapids.name: Apache Falls
rapids.desc: A large, nearly unrunnable ledge a quarter mile above the Highway 60 bridge. Boating upstream of it is prohibited by the White Mountain Apache Tribe.

rapids.name: Island Rapid
rapids.desc: A wave train with holes. Below 1,200 cfs use the First Campground access to avoid it.

rapids.name: Kiss and Tell
rapids.desc: A short drop over a cobble bar just below the put-in.

rapids.name: Bump and Grind
rapids.desc: A drop over a gravel bar. Route choice matters at low water.

rapids.name: Maytag
rapids.desc: An island splits the flow. The deepest channel is river right.

rapids.name: Grumman
rapids.desc: A wave train with a big hole on river left.

rapids.name: Mother Rock
rapids.desc: A boulder in the channel. The main line is right.

rapids.name: Overboard
rapids.desc: A shallow shoal on river left. Run the chute to the far right bank.

rapids.name: Exhibition
rapids.desc: A big wave train with play waves.

rapids.name: Cibecue Rapid
rapids.desc: Formed by outwash from Cibecue Creek.

rapids.name: Three Way
rapids.desc: Islands split the flow, most going river right.

rapids.name: Raft Ripper
rapids.desc: Boulders to avoid, especially at low flows.

rapids.name: Mescal Falls
rapids.desc: A rock-strewn wave train with occasional play holes.

rapids.name: Salt Banks
rapids.desc: A cobble bar pushes the flow right. Saline deposits at the bottom on river right.

rapids.name: Ledges
rapids.desc: Low-angle quartzite ledges with good play waves and holes.

rapids.name: Little Boat Eater
rapids.desc: Avoid the hydraulic on river left over a rock ledge.

rapids.name: Rock Garden
rapids.desc: Many rocks to navigate.

rapids.name: The Cheese
rapids.desc: A cobble bar just above Rat Trap.

rapids.name: Rat Trap
rapids.desc: A long rapid with large exploding waves and holes. The start of the micro canyon. Trip reports describe swims and difficult current crossings.

rapids.name: White Rock
rapids.desc: Polished boulders, boiling eddies, and irregular waves and holes.

rapids.name: Granite
rapids.desc: The largest rapid in the micro gorge, the final drop before Gleason Flat.

rapids.name: Gleason
rapids.desc: A minor rapid above South Gleason access.

rapids.name: Eye of the Needle
rapids.desc: A pinch over a ledge with a powerful hole. Scout river left. Oars have snapped here when not fully stowed.

rapids.name: Black Rock
rapids.desc: The final rapid of a small micro gorge, with sharp boulders and ledges; the line varies with flow. Rafts run near river right over a six-foot pourover; kayaks drop the ledge or punch the hole on river left. An undercut rock follows. Rafts scout from upstream river right, kayaks from river left.

rapids.name: Devils Pendejo
rapids.desc: A huge boulder splits the flow. Rafts go right; hard boats can take slots left.

rapids.name: Upper Corral
rapids.desc: Easy, with boulders and cobbles.

rapids.name: Lower Corral
rapids.desc: A wave train with a huge center hole at higher flows. Marks the boundary of tribal lands and Tonto National Forest.

rapids.name: Pinball
rapids.desc: Large waves, holes and boiling eddies. Do not swim here: it leads into the Maze.

rapids.name: The Maze
rapids.desc: A pair of big holes on river left, then a turn right into a narrow canyon with boiling eddies. Hard to swim or flip here.

rapids.name: Quartzite Falls
rapids.desc: Once Class V, now Class IV after being blasted. A shallow hole at the base on river right can flip loaded rafts. Scout from the ridge on river left. The standard line is center right, with a lateral from the right needing a pivot. A short recovery pool precedes Corkscrew.

rapids.name: Corkscrew
rapids.desc: A complex wave train with a huge hole and exploding waves; rafts can flip at high water. Portage on river left.

rapids.name: Sleeper
rapids.desc: An easy line right after a hole near the top right.

rapids.name: Cliffhanger
rapids.desc: A shoal with a huge rock in the main flow. The eddy on river left is hard to escape in a raft.

rapids.name: Horseshoe Bend
rapids.desc: A gravel bar rapid at a right bend.

rapids.name: Redmond
rapids.desc: A minor riffle, the end of the whitewater.

rapids.name: Diversion Dam
rapids.desc: A 3-foot dam with a lethal hole. Take out at the bridge above it.

hikes.name: Canyon Creek
hikes.desc: A lunch stop and hike; boatable at higher flows.

hikes.name: Cherry Creek
hikes.desc: A side hike with clear water.

hikes.name: Coon Creek
hikes.desc: A side hike; the ridge hike over to Dry and Chalk Creeks takes a few hours.

rules.d: A fire pan with sides at least 3 inches high; all fires stay in it. Self-supporting kayak trips may use a fire blanket.
A portable toilet system. All solid waste is carried out.
A life jacket for each person; the Coast Guard recommends Type III or V.
Collect only dead and down wood. Cutting or stripping limbs is prohibited.
Motorized equipment and boats are prohibited.
Possessing or transporting native plants is prohibited.
Pack out all trash and food remains.
Gear rafts need about 1,200 cfs or more; kayaks and packrafts run down to about 400. Water can rise to flood stage within hours.
Scout Eye of the Needle, Black Rock and Quartzite Falls. Do not swim Pinball into the Maze.
Take out at the Highway 288 bridge. Diversion Dam just below has a lethal hole.
There is no cell service in the canyon.

landmarks.name: First Campground
landmarks.desc: Put-in on river right at the Highway 60 bridge, on Apache Road 1. Separate public and outfitter launches.

landmarks.name: Second Campground
landmarks.desc: A primitive tribal campground with river access.

landmarks.name: Cibecue Creek access
landmarks.desc: Can wash out in Cibecue Creek floods.

landmarks.name: Mescal access
landmarks.desc: Unimproved; the end of the day-trip section.

landmarks.name: Hoodoo access
landmarks.desc: Unimproved; the last option at the end of the day-trip section.

landmarks.name: South Gleason access
landmarks.desc: By a 4WD road off FR 303B. Wilderness boundary: the Tonto wilderness permit applies below this point.

landmarks.name: Tribal land boundary
landmarks.desc: The White Mountain Apache reservation ends and Tonto National Forest begins.

landmarks.name: Horseshoe Bend
landmarks.desc: Alternate access and a tuber launch in summer.

landmarks.name: Highway 288 bridge
landmarks.desc: Take-out on river left just below the bridge, with a ramp. Diversion Dam lies below.

permit.status: Lottery · March 1 to May 15 · plus tribal permit

items.d: Apply on Recreation.gov from December 1 to January 31. One application per person. The lottery application fee is $16, non-refundable ($10 for the Wilderness River Program and $6 reservation).
Lottery winners pay the $125 permit fee by February 20.
Unclaimed dates are first come, first served at $125 plus a reservation fee, and cancelled dates are posted at a random time within 24 hours.
A permit is required from March 1 to May 15 for the wilderness section below South Gleason access.

A tribal permit is required for the roughly 29 miles through the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, from the Highway 60 put-in down to the Tonto National Forest boundary. For multiday trips buy two days. Call 928-338-4385 for costs and rules. The tribe enforces it.
Whitewater boating is prohibited upstream of Apache Falls.
Up to 15 people. The permit holder must be 18 or older and on the trip with the signed permit. Everyone carries photo ID. Non-commercial only.
Launch only on the date on the permit.
Cancel at least 21 days before launch for a refund. To change the date, cancel and rebook.
